section.title: The Righteousness of Faith
section.sectionRationale: Paul now moves from God's sovereign choice to Israel's own responsibility. The stunning result is that Gentiles who never pursued righteousness have obtained it by faith, while Israel, chasing a law of righteousness, failed to reach it, because they sought it by works and stumbled over the stumbling stone. The reason is not that God's word failed but that they were ignorant of God's righteousness and tried to establish their own. Paul then unveils the way of righteousness by faith: Christ is the end and goal of the law, the word of faith is near, and whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised Him will be saved, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, with no distinction between Jew and Greek.
section.thesis: Righteousness comes not by the works of the law but by faith in Christ, who is the end and goal of the law; the saving word is near, so that whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes in his heart that God raised Him will be saved, and this salvation is offered without distinction to everyone who calls on the name of the Lord.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the great reversal, Gentiles attaining righteousness by faith while Israel stumbled over the stone by seeking it through works; Christ the end of the law and Israel's misdirected zeal; and the word of faith, confess and believe and be saved, for everyone who calls on the Lord.

units.label: The great reversal and the stumbling stone
units.note: Gentiles attain righteousness by faith, Israel stumbles

verses.text: What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} that is by faith;
but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it.
Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
as it is written: “See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”

units.label: Christ, the end of the law

verses.text: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation.
For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge.
Because they were ignorant of God's righteousness and sought to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness.
For Christ is the {{telos|end}} of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.

units.label: The word of faith near you
units.note: confess and believe and be saved

verses.text: For concerning the righteousness that is by the law, Moses writes: “The man who does these things will live by them.”
But the righteousness that is by faith says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down)
or, ‘Who will descend into the Abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).”
But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming:
that if you {{homologeo|confess}} with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved.
It is just as the Scripture says: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”
For there is no difference between Jew and Greek: The same {{kyrios|Lord}} is Lord of all, and gives richly to all who call on Him,
for, “Everyone who {{epikaleo|calls on}} the name of the Lord will be saved.”

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, the right standing God requires and gives. Paul contrasts a righteousness pursued by works, which Israel failed to reach, with the righteousness that is by faith, freely received. God's righteousness is not a standard we climb to but a gift bestowed on all who believe, credited apart from the works of the law.

telos.gloss: End, goal, or fulfillment. When Paul says Christ is the telos of the law, he means both that Christ is the terminus of the law as a way of earning righteousness and the goal toward which the law always pointed. In Him the law reaches its intended purpose, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes.

homologeo.gloss: To confess, to say the same thing, to acknowledge openly. To confess that Jesus is Lord is to agree with God's verdict about His Son and to own Him publicly. This confession, joined to heartfelt belief in the resurrection, is the outward voice of a faith that receives salvation.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, sovereign. In the Greek Old Testament kyrios rendered the divine name, so to confess Jesus as Lord is to acknowledge His divine sovereignty and reign. Paul says the same Lord is Lord of all, rich to all who call on Him, applying to Jesus the name and honor of the LORD Himself.

epikaleo.gloss: To call upon, to invoke, to appeal to. Quoting Joel, Paul says everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. To call on the Lord is to turn to Him in faith and cast oneself on His mercy, and this door stands open to all without distinction, Jew and Greek alike.

basic.context: Paul turns from God's sovereign choice in chapter nine to Israel's responsibility. He faces a startling outcome: Gentiles who never sought righteousness have received it by faith, while Israel, zealously pursuing a law of righteousness, failed to attain it. Why? Because they sought it by works rather than faith and stumbled over Christ, the stumbling stone. Paul aches for their salvation, names their sincere but misdirected zeal, and then lays out the way of righteousness by faith in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the flip side of chapter nine. There Paul defended God's freedom; here he presses Israel's real fault. The two truths stand together: God is sovereign, and people are responsible. The heart of the passage is the contrast between establishing your own righteousness and submitting to God's righteousness, received by simple faith in the crucified and risen Christ, whose saving word is near.
basic.originalLanguages: The theme word is dikaiosyne, righteousness, either pursued by works and missed, or received by faith. Christ is the telos of the law, its end and goal. Salvation comes as we homologeo, confess, Jesus as kyrios, Lord, the divine name applied to Him. And it is for everyone who epikaleo, calls on, the name of the Lord.
basic.typology: The stumbling stone laid in Zion, from Isaiah, is fulfilled in Christ, who is both a rock of offense to the unbelieving and a sure foundation to those who trust Him. Moses' words about the nearness of the word, from Deuteronomy, are fulfilled as the gospel of Christ comes near to every heart and mouth.
basic.christ: Christ is the center: He is the stumbling stone over which Israel fell, yet the one in whom no believer is put to shame. He is the end and goal of the law, bringing righteousness to all who believe. He is the Lord to be confessed, raised from the dead, and the same Lord of all, rich to everyone who calls on Him.
basic.god: God is righteous and gives righteousness as a gift. Israel's tragedy was ignoring God's righteousness to build their own. God lays the stone in Zion, brings the word near, justifies the believing heart, and saves all who call, showing no partiality between Jew and Greek. His salvation is generous, near, and free.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 28 and 8 speak of the stone in Zion. Leviticus 18 gives the law's do this and live. Deuteronomy 30 speaks of the word near you. Joel 2 promises salvation to all who call on the name of the LORD.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's long question of how sinners can be righteous before God comes to its clearest answer here. Not by works of the law, at which Israel labored and failed, but by faith in Christ, the end and goal of the law. The saving word is near, and the door stands open to all peoples, so that everyone who calls on the Lord, Jew or Gentile, will be saved.

context.literary:
The passage hangs on a pair of mirrored sections. Romans 9:30 to 33 is a short verdict, put as a question and answer: what shall we say? Gentiles have obtained, Israel has not attained, and the reason is given by a quotation. Chapter 10 then opens up the verdict in two halves. Verses 1 to 4 diagnose the problem, and verses 5 to 13 set two kinds of righteousness side by side, the one that Moses describes in Leviticus and the one that 'says' what Deuteronomy says.

The stumbling stone is the frame. Isaiah's stone is introduced in 9:33 with the promise that the one who believes 'will never be put to shame,' and the same promise returns in 10:11, now with 'anyone' in front of it. Between the two quotations Paul has told the whole story of Israel's failure and the way of faith. Verse 4 is the hinge, with its statement that Christ is the end of the law, and it carries the weight of the argument on either side.

Paul's handling of Deuteronomy 30 in verses 6 to 8 is a distinct literary device. He lets 'the righteousness that is by faith' speak in the first person, as a character in the passage who takes up Moses' own words, and he adds a brief gloss to each phrase with 'that is.' The effect is of a running commentary: ascend to heaven, 'that is, to bring Christ down'; descend to the abyss, 'that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.' The confession and belief of verses 9 and 10 are then set in a chiasm, mouth and heart in verse 9 and heart and mouth in verse 10, with the quotations of verses 11 and 13 binding the section together.
context.historical:
Paul speaks with first hand knowledge of Israel's zeal. He had been 'blameless' in the righteousness of the law, Philippians 3:6, and he had persecuted the church out of that zeal, Galatians 1:13-14. His claim in verse 2 that they are zealous 'but not on the basis of knowledge' is the testimony of someone who was once in the same place.

In the first century many Jews pursued obedience to the law as the mark of covenant faithfulness, in a world where the law was also a boundary that set Israel apart from the Gentile nations. Paul does not mock this. He says they have zeal for God. The issue is that they sought to establish 'their own' righteousness, which can mean a righteousness of their own making, or one that belonged to them alone as a nation. Both senses may be in view, and the second would help explain why the question of Gentiles is so near.

The scene of 'the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness' had a plain meaning for a Roman church. The Gentile believers had come from a world of pagan temples, and had not sought the God of Israel, yet they had been given a righteous standing. For a Jewish Christian that fact was a puzzle. It was not the first time the scandal of grace had been seen, since the early church struggled with it in Acts 10 and 15.

The expression 'call on the name of the Lord' belonged to Israel's worship from early times, Genesis 4:26 and Psalm 116:13, and Peter used Joel's words on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:21. Early Christians soon used it of Jesus, Acts 9:14 and 1 Corinthians 1:2.
context.canonical:
The two stones of Isaiah are put together by Paul. Isaiah 8:14 speaks of the LORD of Hosts Himself as 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' to both houses of Israel, and Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested stone, a precious cornerstone laid in Zion as a sure foundation. Paul sees them as one stone with two effects, and Peter does the same in 1 Peter 2:6-8, adding Psalm 118:22, which Jesus applied to Himself in Matthew 21:42.

Leviticus 18:5 says that a person who keeps the LORD's statutes will live by them, and it appears again in Ezekiel 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:29. Paul quotes it in verse 5 and in Galatians 3:12 to show that the law's own terms are 'do this and live,' a way that no sinner can complete. Elsewhere he insists that the law was good, Romans 7:12, and that it could not give life because of human weakness, Romans 8:3.

Deuteronomy 30:11-14 comes in Moses' last address, in the promise that after the exile God will circumcise their hearts, Deuteronomy 30:6. In its original setting the word that is near is the law itself. Paul hears in it the nearness of the gospel, because Moses had spoken of a heart that is turned and a God who restores. This also fits the way Deuteronomy 9:4 and 10:16 deal with the people's stubbornness.

Joel 2:32 sits in a prophecy of the Spirit being poured out on all flesh, Joel 2:28-32, so that the call to every one who calls is bound up with the new age. Acts 2 brings the pieces together, and Romans 10:13 shows how Paul understood Pentecost to have opened the door to all nations. The theme of faith as the way of righteousness goes back to Genesis 15:6 and Habakkuk 2:4, both already quoted in Romans 1 and 4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted to show that Israel's failure has a cause that is neither the failure of God's word nor mere fate. They pursued righteousness in the wrong way. This gives the lost a responsibility they cannot avoid, and keeps the mystery of chapter 9 from being used as an excuse. He holds both truths together as Scripture does.

He also wants to expose a kind of religion that looks devout and is not. Zeal, sincerity and moral effort can all be present, and still a person may be ignorant of God's righteousness and unwilling to submit to it. For the Jewish reader this was a warning that their best efforts could be the very obstacle, and for the Gentile reader it was a warning not to boast.

And he wants to put the good news within reach. Moses had described a word that is not far off, and Paul says that this word is the gospel. There is no need to climb to heaven or descend to the deep, because Christ has already come down and been raised. All that is left is to believe and to call. The tone throughout is of a pastor who longs for his people to be saved, and he prays for them in verse 1 before he argues.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first half of the passage describes what happened to Israel and what is true of Gentiles. It is a diagnosis and not a command. The second half is more direct: the word of faith is proclaimed, and those who hear are invited to confess and believe. Even there Paul states what saves, in the form of a promise, 'you will be saved,' and does not give a procedure.

Verse 9 is sometimes used as a formula to be recited, and verse 13 as a guarantee that any speaking of the words will do. That misses the setting. The confession Paul names is the heart's allegiance spoken aloud, 'Jesus is Lord,' and the faith is real trust that God raised Him. The verse is a description of the single act of faith in its inward and outward sides, and the call to everyone is a call to real trust.

The reference to Israel's zeal also applies by analogy to anyone today who relies on religious achievement. It is wise to apply it with humility. The text speaks of a particular people who had received the law and missed the Christ it pointed to, and it is not a license to judge others' sincerity.

debates.question: What does it mean that Christ is the 'end' of the law?

views.label: Christ is the goal and fulfilment of the law
views.case: The Greek word telos often means goal or purpose, as in 1 Timothy 1:5. The whole law pointed to Christ, Luke 24:27 and 24:44, and in Him it reaches its aim. This fits Matthew 5:17, where Jesus says He came to fulfill the law and not to abolish it.

views.label: Christ is the termination of the law as a way to righteousness
views.case: The word can also mean end or cessation, and the context is about two ways of righteousness. If righteousness is by faith, then the law as a means of earning it has come to an end for everyone who believes, Galatians 3:23-25. Verse 4 says the end is 'to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.'

views.label: Both ideas are meant at once
views.case: Many hold that Paul intends both goal and end, and that the English word 'end' carries the same double sense. Christ completes what the law aimed at and ends the law's role as a way of earning standing.

debates.bearing: All three agree on the main claim: righteousness is no longer found by doing the law but by faith in Christ, and the law finds its meaning in Him. The point is not that God's moral will has no further place, since the same Paul says that love fulfills the law, Romans 13:8-10.

debates.question: Is confessing with the mouth a second condition added to faith?

views.label: Confession is the outward expression of inward faith
views.case: Verse 10 pairs heart and mouth, and the two work together as a single response. Jesus said that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, Matthew 12:34. Confession is the natural fruit of faith, and faith that never speaks is doubtful.

views.label: Confession is a separate requirement for salvation
views.case: The sentence says that 'with your mouth you confess and are saved,' and some conclude that open acknowledgement is a distinct step, often connected with baptism or public profession. They point to Matthew 10:32 on acknowledging Christ before others.

views.label: Confession marks a person's allegiance to the Lord in the face of cost
views.case: In a world where Caesar was called lord, saying 'Jesus is Lord' was dangerous. On this view Paul is describing the response of those who are willing to stand with Christ despite the cost.

debates.bearing: Paul places faith in the heart as the ground and puts justification first in verse 10. Nowhere does he suggest that salvation is earned by speech, and verse 11 quotes Isaiah on belief alone. The passage teaches that real faith will not stay silent.

study.originalLanguages:
The passage begins with the phrase 'law of righteousness' in 9:31, a nomos dikaiosynes. It names the law as the thing pursued, as though Israel chased the law itself and not the God behind it. The verb 'pursue' is dioko, the same word used for hunting down or persecuting, and Paul uses it of both the Gentiles, who 'did not pursue,' and Israel. It is the word Paul used of himself as a persecutor, Philippians 3:6. The irony is that those who ran hardest did not arrive. The verb 'attain' is phthano, to arrive at a goal.

The stone of verse 32 is lithos proskommatos, 'stone of stumbling,' and the 'rock of offense' is petra skandalou, where skandalon is the trap or snare that trips a person. These come from Isaiah 8:14. The clause 'will never be put to shame' comes from the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 28:16, which reads kataischyno, 'to be put to shame.' The Hebrew of that verse speaks of one who believes not being in haste or panic, and Paul follows the Greek text. In 10:11 he adds the word 'anyone,' which is not in Isaiah, to bring out the universal reach.

In verse 2 the word 'knowledge' is epignosis, a full and exact knowledge. Their zeal lacked that. In verse 3, 'ignorant' is agnoeo, 'not knowing,' and the verb 'submit' is hypotasso, the same verb used of the mind of the flesh in Romans 8:7, which 'does not submit to God's law.' The word 'establish' is histemi, to set up or stand, and the contrast is with receiving: they tried to set up their own, instead of accepting the gift.

The word telos in verse 4 can mean end, goal, outcome or completion. It appears in Romans 6:21 and 6:22 of the outcome of a way of life, and in 1 Timothy 1:5 of the aim of a charge. English 'end' preserves some of the ambiguity, and in the Greek it comes first in the sentence, in an emphatic position.

In verse 5 the words 'the man who does these things will live by them' echo the Greek of Leviticus 18:5, and the verb 'do' is poieo, the emphasis falling on doing. In verses 6 to 8 Paul changes the Deuteronomy text in notable ways. Moses wrote 'Who will cross the sea for us,' Deuteronomy 30:13, and Paul writes 'Who will descend into the Abyss,' abyssos, the deep, and applies it to Christ's resurrection. The phrase 'that is' marks Paul's own running comment on the text.

In verse 9 the verb 'confess' is homologeo, literally 'say the same thing,' to agree and affirm. The confession is kyrios Iesous, 'Jesus is Lord.' In the Greek Old Testament kyrios is the word that stands for the name of the LORD, and when verse 13 applies Joel's 'call on the name of the Lord' to Him, the identification is complete. The 'believe' is pisteuo, and the 'raised' is egeiro in the aorist. In verse 10 'justified' is the verb dikaioo and 'saved' is sozo.

The verb 'call on' in verse 13 is epikaleo, which in the middle voice means to appeal to or invoke, as in appealing to a higher court, Acts 25:11. In verse 12 the word 'difference' is diastole, a separation, and Paul has used it before in 3:22, 'there is no distinction.'

typology.type: The stone laid in Zion, Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah speaks of the LORD as a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling, and of a tested cornerstone laid in Zion for those who trust. The words apply to the temple city. In Christ the stone becomes a Person, who is the foundation of the church, Ephesians 2:20, and the living stone chosen by God, 1 Peter 2:4-8. The correspondence is of one stone with two effects, safety for those who rest on it and a fall for those who trip over it. The type falls short because Zion's stone was a promise of security in the city, while Christ is both a foundation and a judge, Luke 20:17-18.

typology.type: The word near in the mouth and in the heart, Deuteronomy 30:14
typology.fulfillment: Moses told Israel that the commandment was not too hard or too far, but very near. Paul says that this nearness is realised in the message of Christ, 'the word of faith we are proclaiming.' The correspondence is of God's revelation brought close. In Christ it becomes personal, since 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,' John 1:14. The type is surpassed because the law could be heard but could not give life, whereas the gospel brings the One who is the life. The nearness is also given by the Spirit, who writes on hearts, 2 Corinthians 3:3.

typology.type: Moses' righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 18:5 sets out a way of life by doing, and Deuteronomy 30 speaks of a way marked by return and trust. Paul places them side by side. The pattern is that the law described the life of obedience that Christ lived in full, Matthew 5:17 and Galatians 4:4-5, and the faith that receives Him is the faith Abraham had before the law, Romans 4:9-12. The correspondence is that what the law required is given through Christ, Romans 8:3-4. The type falls short because Moses could set life before the people, but could not give them the heart to take it, Deuteronomy 29:4.

typology.type: The Lord's name called upon, Joel 2:32
typology.fulfillment: In Joel the call on the LORD's name is the means of rescue on the day of judgment, in the midst of Zion. Peter proclaims at Pentecost that the day has dawned and the Spirit is poured out, Acts 2:17-21. The correspondence is of rescue for all who call, and the escalation is that the Lord on whose name they call is Jesus, Romans 10:9. It is also widened beyond Zion to every nation, Romans 10:12. The pattern is still unfinished, since the day of the Lord in its fullness is yet to come, and the call goes on until then.

study.christ:
Romans 9:30 to 10:13 is about Christ in every sentence, though it names Him directly only a few times. He is first the stone. Israel stumbled over the stone laid in Zion, and Paul, with Peter, identifies it as Christ, the One who in His weakness and cross was an offense, 1 Corinthians 1:23. The people stumbled because they sought righteousness by works and the cross put all works aside. Yet the same stone is the foundation of all who believe, and 'will never be put to shame.'

Christ is the end of the law. The word has the sense of goal and of termination at once, and Paul's context is that of righteousness. He is the goal because He fulfills what the law demanded and what it promised, as Jesus said that all the Scriptures speak of Him, Luke 24:27 and John 5:39. He is the end because the way of earning righteousness through the law has been replaced for those who believe by the gift of His righteousness, 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Philippians 3:9. The phrase 'to bring righteousness to everyone who believes' states the purpose of the whole.

Christ is the one in whom the word of Deuteronomy comes near. Paul says no one needs to bring Him down from heaven, for the incarnation has happened, and no one needs to bring Him up from the dead, for the resurrection has happened. In those two phrases the story of the gospel is told: He came down and He was raised, Philippians 2:6-11. The message that is preached is Him, John 1:14 and Colossians 1:27.

He is the Lord who is confessed. The confession 'Jesus is Lord' makes Him the Lord, kyrios, the title of God in the Greek Bible. Paul can then apply to Him the words of Joel about calling on the LORD. This is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that the early church worshiped Jesus as God. It is the confession that no one can make except by the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12:3, and it will be made by every tongue at the last, Philippians 2:10-11.

He is the Lord of all who is rich to all who call, verse 12. The riches are those of His grace, Ephesians 3:8, and they are open to Jew and Gentile alike.

A caution applies to Paul's use of Deuteronomy. He is not saying that Moses secretly wrote about the resurrection. He is showing that the same God who spoke nearness in the law has brought it to its goal in Christ, and that the language of the law now finds its fullest sense there.
study.god:
The passage shows a God whose righteousness is a gift. The tragedy Paul names is that Israel did not know 'God's righteousness,' and set about making their own. The phrase refers to the righteousness that God requires, that God gives, and that belongs to God as His own character. The God of this passage does not hold out a standard and wait to see who reaches it. He supplies the righteousness in Christ and invites everyone to receive it.

He is a God who lays the stone Himself. 'I lay in Zion a stone,' verse 33. The stumbling is not an accident that surprises Him, and the foundation is His provision. This is a God who plans both the offense and the remedy, in His own wisdom, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 1:21-25.

He is near. The word is 'in your mouth and in your heart.' The distance between God and people, which the law made so keenly felt, has been closed by Him. This is the God who, in Deuteronomy, circumcises the heart, and in the gospel shines light into hearts, 2 Corinthians 4:6.

He is impartial and generous. 'There is no difference between Jew and Greek.' He is the same Lord of all, and 'gives richly to all who call on Him.' The word 'richly' is a word of overflow, not of grudging supply. Neither ancestry, nor the law, nor moral record sets one person ahead of another before Him. He is God of the Gentiles also, Romans 3:29.

He is a God who holds people responsible. The first half of the passage shows God's sovereign choice in the chapter before, and the second shows that Israel did not submit and that people must call on Him. The Bible does not play the two truths against each other. God is free, and He is also just in holding people to account. He is also a God who is grieved, as Paul is in 10:1, and who stretches out His hands all day long to a disobedient people, which is the verse Paul quotes at the end of this chapter, 10:21.

He is a God who saves by the resurrection. The faith that saves is faith in the God who raised Jesus from the dead, so His power over death is part of the content of the gospel, Romans 4:24.

For worship, the passage calls for humility, since no one can boast of what is received, and for confidence, since the call is answered. It also sends us to those who have not yet called, since the God who is rich to all wants to be called on by all.

crossReferences.note: The LORD lays in Zion a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation, and the one who believes will not be shaken. Paul quotes it in 9:33 and in 10:11, and the repeated quotation holds the whole passage together.

The LORD of Hosts will be a sanctuary, and also a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel. It is combined with Isaiah 28:16 in Romans 9:33 and shows that the same stone is both refuge and ruin, depending on whether one trusts.

Keep My statutes and ordinances, for the man who does them will live by them. Paul quotes it in 10:5 as the principle of the law, which he contrasts with the righteousness of faith, and Galatians 3:12 uses it the same way.

The commandment is not too hard or far off, for the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart. Paul takes Moses' language and shows that it points to the gospel, which is near in the preaching of Christ.

Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Paul quotes it in 10:13 and Peter in Acts 2:21, and in both it is applied to Jesus, which makes the point that the Lord whom believers call on is the Lord who is God.

Paul lists his own record of zeal and law keeping, and counts it as loss for the sake of a righteousness that comes through faith in Christ and not from his own law. It is the personal side of Romans 10:2-4.

Those who rely on works of the law are under a curse, and Christ redeemed us from it, so that the blessing might come to the Gentiles. The argument runs on the same lines as Romans 10, and quotes Leviticus 18:5 in the same way.

Peter quotes Joel on the day of Pentecost, 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' It shows the verse at the dawn of the church, where it opens the door to all who hear, which Paul takes up in Romans 10:12-13.

Peter combines Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14 to describe Christ as the cornerstone for believers and a stone of stumbling for those who disobey. It confirms that the early church read the stone texts as Paul did.

The righteousness of God has been made known apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe, since there is no distinction. It is the main statement of the doctrine that Romans 10 returns to and applies to Israel's case.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's central question is how a holy God can be near to sinful people, and this passage gives a compact answer. From the garden, people have tried to cover themselves, with fig leaves and later with religious achievement, and God has answered by providing the covering Himself. Israel received the law as a gift, a way of life in the covenant, yet it was also meant to show their need, Romans 3:20, and to lead to the Christ, Galatians 3:24. When Israel took the law as a means of establishing their own standing, they missed the one it was pointing to.

The passage ties together the long story of faith. Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, Genesis 15:6, centuries before the law. Habakkuk said that the righteous will live by faith. David sang of the one whose sin is covered, Psalm 32:1-2. Paul says that this stream of faith, which runs under the whole Old Testament, has come to its full flow in Christ.

It also stands at the hinge between Israel and the nations. The stone laid in Zion becomes a foundation for people from every nation, and the call of Joel reaches beyond Israel, since the Lord is Lord of all. This was God's purpose from the beginning, when He promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3.

It sets up the next step in Romans. Verses 14 to 21 say how people will call, which is by hearing, which is by preaching, so the passage opens the sending of the church to the world. Chapter 11 will show that the story of Israel is not over.

The ending is the same at which Philippians 2 arrives, with every knee bowed and every tongue confessing that Jesus Christ is Lord, and the shame that came in with Adam is gone for those who trusted in Him. Revelation shows the multitude from every nation who called on the Lord and were saved, and who stand clothed in the righteousness He gave them, Revelation 7:9-14.

quiz.q: Why did Israel fail to attain the righteousness they pursued?

options.text: Because they pursued it not by faith but as if it were by works, and stumbled over the stumbling stone, Christ.
options.note: Verses 32 and 33 name the cause: seeking righteousness by works and stumbling over Christ.

options.text: Because they did not try hard enough to keep the law.
options.note: Their zeal was real; the fault was the wrong method, works instead of faith.

options.text: Because God gave them no opportunity to believe.
options.note: God laid the stone and brought the word near; the fault was unbelief, not lack of opportunity.

options.text: Because the law itself was evil.
options.note: The law is not evil; Israel misused it as a way of works rather than pointing to Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean that Christ is the end of the law?

options.text: Christ is the end and goal of the law, so that righteousness now comes to everyone who believes, not by law keeping.
options.note: Verse 4: Christ terminates the law as a way of earning righteousness and fulfills its aim.

options.text: Christ made the moral distinctions of right and wrong meaningless.
options.note: Christ does not abolish righteousness; He brings it to all who believe.

options.text: Christ merely reformed the law into stricter rules.
options.note: The point is not stricter rules but righteousness by faith in Him.

options.text: Christ is the goal the law pointed to, though it can still justify by works.
options.note: He is the goal, but Paul denies that the law can justify by works at all.

quiz.q: According to verse 9, how is a person saved?

options.text: By confessing with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believing in the heart that God raised Him from the dead.
options.note: Verse 9 joins heartfelt faith in the resurrection with the confession of Jesus as Lord.

options.text: By reciting the right words regardless of what the heart believes.
options.note: Confession must be joined to heart belief; it is faith finding its voice, not mere words.

options.text: By keeping the law well enough to earn God's approval.
options.note: Paul contrasts this saving faith with the failed pursuit of righteousness by works.

options.text: By being born a Jew and observing the covenant signs.
options.note: Paul says there is no difference between Jew and Greek; salvation is by faith.

quiz.q: What does it mean to confess that Jesus is Lord?

options.text: To acknowledge His divine sovereignty, applying to Jesus the name and honor of the LORD Himself.
options.note: Kyrios rendered the divine name; the same Lord is Lord of all, rich to all who call.

options.text: To treat Jesus as one good teacher among many.
options.note: The confession names Him Lord of all, not merely a teacher.

options.text: To recognize Him only as a human master.
options.note: Kyrios here carries the weight of the divine name, not merely an earthly master.

options.text: To submit to Him as a political ruler.
options.note: His lordship is divine and saving, not merely political.

quiz.q: Who may be saved according to verses 12 and 13?

options.text: Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, with no difference between Jew and Greek.
options.note: The same Lord is Lord of all, rich to all who call, quoting Joel's open promise.

options.text: Only those descended from Abraham.
options.note: Paul says there is no difference between Jew and Greek.

options.text: Only those who first keep the whole law.
options.note: Salvation comes by calling on the Lord in faith, not by law keeping.

options.text: Only a select few chosen at random.
options.note: The invitation is genuinely open to everyone who calls, though salvation rests on God's mercy.

questions: Israel was zealous for God but not according to knowledge, and built their own righteousness. Where might your religious effort be an attempt to establish your own righteousness rather than submitting to God's?
Christ is the end and goal of the law. How does resting in Him as the finish of all your striving change the way you relate to God's commands?
The word of faith is near you, in your mouth and heart. How does the nearness and simplicity of the gospel comfort you when you are tempted to think salvation is out of reach?
Salvation comes by confessing Jesus as Lord and believing He is risen. Is there an area of your life where confessing Jesus as Lord openly would cost you something this week?
Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, with no distinction. How does the width of this promise shape the way you pray for and speak to people very different from you?

translationNotes.note: End of the law renders telos, which can mean termination or goal. Christ is both the end of the law as a way to earn righteousness and the goal to which it pointed; the two senses reinforce one another.

Jesus is Lord renders the confession Kyrios Iesous. Since kyrios translated the divine name in the Greek Old Testament, the confession ascribes divine sovereignty to Jesus, matching the same Lord is Lord of all in verse 12.

Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved quotes Joel 2:32, where the name is the LORD; Paul applies it to Jesus, a striking witness to His deity and to the universal offer of the gospel.
